```{r not-available, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !ok}

This article compares three soft clusterings of the same patients with the
widths of **Silhouette**, and then uses the known diagnoses to check what the
widths reveal. It follows the thyroid example of the package paper and shows
the full code.

The UCI thyroid data, distributed with **mclust** [@mclust2016], record five
laboratory measurements on 215 patients whose thyroid function was diagnosed
from their full medical record as normal, hypothyroid or hyperthyroid.

```{r library}
library(Silhouette)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(mclust))
data(thyroid, package = "mclust")
table(thyroid$Diagnosis)
Xt <- scale(thyroid[, -1])   # standardized laboratory measurements
```

# Three soft clusterings

We fit three methods with $K = 3$: fuzzy c-means [@bezdek1981] from
**ppclust**, a Gaussian mixture from **mclust** whose covariance structure is
chosen by BIC, and probabilistic distance clustering adjusted for cluster size
[PDQ, @iyigun2008] from **FPDclustering** [@fpdclustering2025]. The diagnoses
are not used in fitting.

```{r fits}
set.seed(1)
fc <- ppclust::fcm(Xt, centers = 3, nstart = 5)
gm <- Mclust(Xt, G = 3, verbose = FALSE)
pq <- FPDclustering::PDQ(Xt, k = 3)
```

For each fit we need two $215 \times 3$ matrices: the Euclidean distances from
each patient to each cluster center, and the membership or posterior
probabilities. `ppclust::fcm()` stores squared distances, so we take square
roots.

```{r matrices}
fits <- list(
  FCM = list(prox = sqrt(fc$d), prob = fc$u),
  GMM = list(prox = as.matrix(proxy::dist(Xt, t(gm$parameters$mean))), prob = gm$z),
  PDQ = list(prox = as.matrix(proxy::dist(Xt, pq$centers)), prob = pq$probability))
labels <- lapply(fits, function(f) max.col(f$prob))   # the partition each method produced
```

# Average widths

For the distance-based widths we pass the memberships as `prob_matrix`, so
that every patient keeps the cluster the method assigned (passing
`cluster = labels[[...]]` would do the same). For the probability-based widths
we pass the memberships alone. The density-based width warns about zero
posteriors, which are discussed below, so its warnings are suppressed here.

```{r averages}
avg <- function(s) summary(s, print.summary = FALSE)$avg.width
tab <- sapply(fits, function(f) c(
  medoid     = avg(Silhouette(f$prox, prob_matrix = f$prob)),
  pac        = avg(Silhouette(f$prox, prob_matrix = f$prob, method = "pac")),
  pp_pac     = avg(softSilhouette(f$prob)),
  nlpp_pac   = avg(softSilhouette(f$prob, prob_type = "nlpp")),
  cer        = avg(cerSilhouette(f$prob)),
  db         = avg(suppressWarnings(dbSilhouette(f$prob, average = "crisp")))))
ari <- sapply(labels, adjustedRandIndex, thyroid$Diagnosis)
knitr::kable(rbind(tab, ARI_with_diagnosis = ari), digits = 3)
```

```{r averages-values, include = FALSE}
ord <- function(v) paste(names(sort(v, decreasing = TRUE)), collapse = ", ")
```

The two families of widths rank the methods differently. The distance-based
widths rank them `r ord(tab["medoid", ])`, and the probability-based widths
rank them `r ord(tab["pp_pac", ])`. Agreement with the diagnosis, which would
not be available in practice, orders them `r ord(ari)`.

The difference is expected. Distances to cluster means reward the spherical,
equal-spread clusters that fuzzy c-means looks for, while the mixture (here
with covariance model `r gm$modelName`) allows clusters of different shapes;
posterior probabilities reward decisive assignment, which the mixture
achieves. In this example the probability-based widths pointed to the
partition that matches the diagnosis, but neither family is a substitute for
knowing what kind of cluster the analysis is after.

The distance-based and probability-based widths agree on PDQ: every one of them
is lowest for it. With the default initialization, PDQ placed
`r max(table(labels$PDQ))` of the 215 patients in one cluster; five random
initializations gave similar partitions, all with an adjusted Rand index below
0.05.

```{r db-scale, include = FALSE}
log_ratio <- function(p) apply(p, 1, function(z) { s <- sort(z, decreasing = TRUE); log(s[1] / s[2]) })
max_finite <- sapply(fits, function(f) { r <- log_ratio(f$prob); max(r[is.finite(r)]) })
```

The density-based width is the exception, and it is lowest for the mixture.
Each density-based width is divided by the largest finite log ratio in the
sample. For the mixture that log ratio is about
`r round(max_finite["GMM"])`, against `r round(max_finite["FCM"], 1)` for fuzzy
c-means, so most of the mixture's widths are divided by a very large number.
The density-based average for the mixture therefore reflects its few most
confident patients more than the partition; see the section on zero posteriors
below.

The same table, with fuzzy and median averages as well, comes from
`calSilhouette()`, which scores the partition given by the memberships in every
row:

```{r calsil}
cs <- suppressWarnings(calSilhouette(prox_matrix = fits$GMM$prox, prob_matrix = fits$GMM$prob))
cs
all.equal(cs$Crisp[cs$Method == "medoid"], unname(tab["medoid", "GMM"]))
```

Scoring the distances without the memberships would assign every patient to
the nearest center instead, a different partition for these fits:

```{r relabel}
sapply(fits, function(f) sum(max.col(f$prob) != max.col(-f$prox)))
```

# Which patients are poorly clustered?

The individual widths are more useful than the averages. To check them, we map
each cluster to its majority diagnosis and mark the patients whose diagnosis
differs.

```{r misassigned}
wrong <- lapply(labels, function(l) {
  majority <- apply(table(l, thyroid$Diagnosis), 1, which.max)
  levels(thyroid$Diagnosis)[majority[as.character(l)]] != as.character(thyroid$Diagnosis)
})
sapply(wrong, sum)
```

```{r strip, fig.alt = "Two strip charts of per-patient widths for FCM, GMM and PDQ. In the distance-based panel, patients whose cluster disagrees with the diagnosis sit mostly at low or negative widths for FCM and GMM. In the probability-based panel, GMM widths are almost all near 1, including most disagreeing patients. PDQ widths are low throughout."}
w_med <- lapply(fits, function(f) Silhouette(f$prox, prob_matrix = f$prob)$sil_width)
w_pp <- lapply(fits, function(f) softSilhouette(f$prob)$sil_width)
st <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(nm) rbind(
  data.frame(method = nm, panel = "distance-based (medoid)", width = w_med[[nm]],
             wrong = wrong[[nm]]),
  data.frame(method = nm, panel = "probability-based (pp, PAC)", width = w_pp[[nm]],
             wrong = wrong[[nm]]))))
st$status <- factor(ifelse(st$wrong, "disagrees with diagnosis", "agrees with diagnosis"),
                    c("agrees with diagnosis", "disagrees with diagnosis"))
st <- st[order(st$wrong), ]   # draw disagreeing patients on top

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(3)
ggplot(st, aes(method, width, colour = status, shape = status)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.22, height = 0, size = 1.4, alpha = 0.85) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Silhouette width") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Because the labels come from the memberships, a patient whose assigned cluster
is not the nearest center has a negative medoid width. To compare the widths
with the diagnoses, we take the tenth of patients with the smallest widths and
compare the share of misassigned patients among them with the share among the
rest:

```{r deciles}
low_share <- function(w, bad) {
  low <- w <= quantile(w, 0.1)
  c(lowest_tenth = mean(bad[low]), others = mean(bad[!low]))
}
round(rbind(
  medoid_FCM = low_share(w_med$FCM, wrong$FCM),
  medoid_GMM = low_share(w_med$GMM, wrong$GMM),
  pp_GMM = low_share(w_pp$GMM, wrong$GMM)), 2)
```

By rank, both families point to the same patients: misassigned patients are
concentrated among the smallest widths. In absolute terms they do not. For the
mixture, the misassigned patients' probability-based widths are still high,

```{r medians}
c(misassigned = median(w_pp$GMM[wrong$GMM]), others = median(w_pp$GMM[!wrong$GMM]))
```

so the mixture is confidently wrong about them, whereas their medoid widths
place them among the poorly separated patients:

```{r medians-medoid}
c(misassigned = median(w_med$GMM[wrong$GMM]), others = median(w_med$GMM[!wrong$GMM]))
```

In practice, the patients with the smallest widths are the ones to review
first. The object keeps the rows in the order of the data, so they are easy to
list:

```{r review}
sil_gmm <- Silhouette(fits$GMM$prox, prob_matrix = fits$GMM$prob)
worst <- order(sil_gmm$sil_width)[1:8]
data.frame(patient = worst, cluster = sil_gmm$cluster[worst],
           width = round(sil_gmm$sil_width[worst], 3),
           diagnosis = thyroid$Diagnosis[worst])
```

# The density-based width and zero posteriors

The density-based width of @menardi2011density scales each log ratio
$\log(\gamma_{ic_i}/\gamma_{i\nu_i})$ by the largest one in the sample. For
some patients the mixture's posterior probability of the neighboring component
underflows to exactly zero:

```{r zeros}
sum(apply(gm$z, 1, function(z) sort(z, decreasing = TRUE)[2]) == 0)
```

Their log ratios are infinite. `dbSilhouette()` gives these patients width 1,
scales the other widths by the largest finite log ratio, and says so in a
warning. (Up to version 0.9.6, the infinite maximum made every other width
zero.)

```{r db}
db_gmm <- dbSilhouette(gm$z, average = "crisp")
avg(db_gmm)
```

The average is still small, because the largest finite log ratios of the
mixture are huge and set the scale for everyone else. The individual
density-based widths still rank the patients by how decisively they are
assigned, but the average of a mixture with near-zero posteriors should not be
compared with that of a method without them.

# Fuzzy averaging

With `average = "fuzzy"`, each width is weighted by
$(\gamma_{i(1)} - \gamma_{i(2)})^a$, the gap between the two largest
memberships [@campello2006fuzzy]. For the fuzzy
c-means memberships the average depends clearly on the exponent:

```{r exponent}
sapply(c(a0.5 = 0.5, a1 = 1, a2 = 2, a4 = 4), function(a)
  avg(softSilhouette(fc$u, average = "fuzzy", a = a)))
```

Larger exponents shift weight toward decisively assigned patients, so fuzzy
averages are comparable only at the same `a`.

# Lessons

- Compute each width for every fit and compare fits within a width, never
  widths with each other.
- Distance-based and probability-based widths answer different questions and
  can rank methods differently. Report both when the methods assume different
  cluster shapes.
- A method that fails, like PDQ here, is flagged by the distance-based and the
  probability-based widths alike.
- Use the individual widths to find the observations to review, and pass the
  memberships as `prob_matrix` (or the labels as `cluster`) so that the widths
  refer to the partition the method produced.
- Read the density-based average with care when posteriors are near zero: the
  most extreme patients set its scale.
